doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Keeping a working group together
summary: The value of a steady band, with Harry Allen and Diana Krall as examples.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Right. It’s nice to see a group that has had a personnel, a group of people that have been together for a while.

You know because too often you go to the clubs even and you pay quite a bit of money to get in and you’re looking at good musicians, but it’s not a band. And sometimes you feel a little bit, well this is personal, sometimes I feel a little bit cheated when I’m looking over and I’m seeing somebody tell chord changes to somebody.

Yeah. Oh I mean I think it’s hard. Harry Allen is one of my dearest friends. He’s a great tenor saxophone player. And he’ll go out and work with Bill Charlap and Kenny Washington and Peter Washington, and I know he lives and dies by his book. He goes around the world and plays with like a drummer and a bass player somewhere in England, and luckily he’s got Charlap and they have a bit of a vibe. But I know he’s got to put out those charts and you know everybody’s got to know what they’re doing. But actually Bill’s been pretty good with them, but I mean it’s a hard thing to be one guy and have to — you’re not going to get Bill Charlap all over the world. So at least Bill can sort of go okay, I see where you’re headed, and sort of go like that and you know you’re going to hear everything come out right. But I’m struggling to keep the group together just because that’s the key. I mean Diana Krall, we have talked about that too, is that she’s had to change personnel. And it’s hard to have two guys who know the book on the guitar. And to find guys that can play rhythm guitar. She says they don’t know songs. And does anybody play any time? It’s just about getting up there and swinging hard. And nobody wants to do that. It’s square. It’s not this it’s not that. So I’m very lucky to have Ray Kennedy and Martin. Well Martin, he has to do it, there’s no other option for Martin. But that’s the key. I mean we go anywhere. We’ve got about 150, 200 things in our
brains. We just go zip, zip and it works. So I agree with you about groups, to make a long story longer.
